Outcome: mean symptom score at week 12
Report: Of 200 randomized in each arm, approximately nine in each arm lacked a week-12 score. Exact counts await reconciliation; most missed visits followed clinic closures. The mean difference was 0.2 points on a 0–100 scale; observed SD was 18.

Outcome: mean symptom score at week 12
Report: The ITT mixed model estimated a difference of 0.2 points. Two hundred patients were randomized per arm. Visits were scheduled at week 12; actual score collection and losses are not reported.

Distinguish availability, possible outcome dependence, likely outcome dependence, and evidence that missing outcomes did not bias the result. Explain supported inferences and limits.
Outcome: mean symptom score at week 12
Report: Nine of 200 participants per arm lacked a score. Recorded clinic closures caused all missing visits. A sensitivity analysis assigned missing scores across the clinically plausible 20–80 range separately in each arm; the large estimated treatment difference changed by less than one point.

Distinguish availability, possible outcome dependence, likely outcome dependence, and evidence that missing outcomes did not bias the result. Explain supported inferences and limits.
Outcome: mean symptom score at week 12
Report: Approximate missing-score rates were 20% versus 5%. Patients commonly declined assessment because symptoms worsened. Last observation carried forward was used; no assumptions about subsequent worsening were examined.

Outcome: death by day 90
Report: Vital status was known for approximately 98% of 500 participants per arm. Exact day-90 counts were not reconciled; follow-up calls and registry searches identified deaths. About ten deaths were recorded per arm.

Outcome: death by day 90
Report: Five hundred patients were randomized per arm; ITT mortality risk ratios are reported. A registry search was planned. The number with known day-90 vital status and actual searches are not reported.

Outcome: infection by day 30
Report: Only two of 400 participants per arm lacked day-30 infection assessment because laboratory samples were accidentally destroyed. Both best- and worst-case assignments for these outcomes left the estimated clinically substantial risk difference essentially unchanged.

Outcome: infection by day 30
Report: Approximately 8% versus 1% lacked outcome ascertainment; many unassessed participants were hospitalized elsewhere for suspected infection. Recorded infection rates were 3% versus 2%. ITT analysis was claimed without a missing-outcome sensitivity result.

Outcome: time to first cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke through trial closeout
Report: Observed/expected endpoint follow-up was approximately 95% in both arms. Vital status was known for 99%; some non-completers without a recorded first event withdrew consent. Outcome follow-up generally continued after treatment stopped; individual loss timing is unavailable.

Outcome: time to first cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke through trial closeout
Report: All randomized patients were included in the Cox analysis. The censoring rule used last endpoint contact. Vital status was known for 99%, but actual composite-outcome follow-up, nonfatal ascertainment and losses were not reported.

Distinguish availability, possible outcome dependence, likely outcome dependence, and evidence that missing outcomes did not bias the result. Explain supported inferences and limits.
Outcome: time to first cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke through trial closeout
Report: Complete endpoint follow-up continued after treatment cessation for nearly all participants. Small actual follow-up losses were similar by arm and followed documented site closures. Performed missing-follow-up event imputations across clinically plausible arm-specific hazards did not materially change the estimate.

Outcome: time to first cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke through trial closeout
Report: Endpoint follow-up stopped on treatment withdrawal for about 20% versus 5%. Withdrawal frequently followed worsening cardiovascular status. Vital status was later recovered for most participants. The SAP planned a tipping-point analysis; only ITT and on-treatment estimates are reported.
